title: Damien of Molokai (1840–1889)
hookLine: a Belgian priest serves the leprosy settlement on Molokai and, tradition says, begins his sermons we lepers

cards: On the island of Molokai, in Hawaii, a flat green peninsula sits at the foot of tall sea cliffs: sea in front, a wall of rock behind. The Hawaiian kingdom sent people with leprosy there, by law, to live apart.
Families were split on the docks, and those sent were not expected back. A young priest from Belgium, already working on the islands, offers to go. He lands with very little.
Tradition says that for years his sermons began my brethren. Then, one Sunday, they began with two different words.

teach.b: His name was Jozef De Veuster. In religious life he took the name Damien, as a member of the Congregation of the Sacred Hearts. The Church now calls him Saint Damien of Molokai.
First, the work. The settlement on the Kalaupapa peninsula needed everything. Damien dressed wounds, built houses and helped build a church.
He dug graves and made coffins, so the dying could be buried with dignity. He organized care for orphaned children. Second, the nearness.
He did not keep a careful distance. He ate with the people, shared his pipe, touched the sick.
In Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus describes the Son of man welcoming those who cared for him: "sick, and you visited me." In the Latin of the Vulgate, sick is infirmus.
Damien took the visiting part to its end. Third, the two words. In time Damien found that he had the disease himself.

teach.h: FROM MY BRETHREN TO WE LEPERS.
teach.b: Tradition says that from then on, he began his sermons not my brethren, but we lepers. No longer one who visits. One of them.

He kept working as long as he could, and died on Molokai, among the people he had come to serve. A word about the word. Leprosy is what the disease was called then, and it is in the saint's own sentence.
Today it is called Hansen's disease, and it can be cured.
Some people who have lived with it have asked not to be called lepers, and his line is honored as his, not as a label for anyone else.

how: Catholics in Hawaii keep Saint Damien's feast on May 10, and parishes and shrines named for him remember him as a friend of people with Hansen's disease.

games.q: you are a young priest on the islands. the bishop needs someone for the leprosy settlement, from which people are not expected to return. what do you do?
o: stay where you are; someone else will go.
visit once a year by boat.
games.why: Damien offered to go. he stayed, caught the disease, and died there among the people.

practice: Who is sent to the edge where you live: someone sick, someone old and alone, someone everyone avoids?

Let one face come to mind and, without fixing anything, stand beside them in your imagination, the way Damien stood beside the people of Kalaupapa, noticing what changes when you say we instead of they.
If you pray, pray for that person by name; if you don't, simply hold them in mind.

wordCard.voice: Kalaupapa. The peninsula in Hawaii where people with leprosy were sent, and where Damien of Molokai built houses, dug graves, and died among them.

orig.note: Latin for sick, from Matthew 25:36 in the Vulgate: sick, and you visited me.

carryVoice: Your line: we lepers. Two small words, and a whole life given behind them. Until tomorrow.
